newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada auto union choses GM as next bargaining target.
newsitem.headline: Canada auto union choses GM as next bargaining target.

text.p: The Canadian Auto Workers (CAW) union said on Monday it chose General Motors Corp.'s Canadian unit as the union's next bargaining target, with a strike deadline set for midnight on Oct. 2.

One day after CAW members overwhelmingly ratified a tentative agreement reached last week with Chrysler Corp.'s Canadian unit, the union said it is now set to do battle to ensure the terms will be applied to any labour deal with General Motors Canada.
"GM will accept the pattern," CAW president Buzz Hargrove told a news conference on Monday. "The only question is when."
But GM lead negotiator, Dean Munger, said he hoped to craft an agreement tailored to GM's own business plans, which include decisions to sell two plants and contract out more than 5,000 CAW jobs.
"We have to take a look at our business plan and see how that fits in line with what Chrysler did," Munger said.
Hargrove asserted that GM is mistaken if it believes the deal on outsourcing with Chrysler was tied to a business plan or if GM believes it can change the language of the deal.

"They think somehow Chrysler's decision (agreement) was tied to their business plan and that's absolute hogwash," Hargrove said. "They wanted to tailor it to the business plan and we detached it from the business plan."

The language on outsourcing -- or farming out work to outside contractors -- in the Chrysler agreement stipulates that the company cannot reduce the number of CAW jobs as a result of outsourcing. It includes a moratorium on the sale or closure of plants during the life of the agreement.
Outsourcing is broadly defined as the sale or closure of plants or the transfer of work to outside contractors whose employees are generally not members of the auto unions.
CAW president Buzz Hargrove said the union is determined to reverse GM's plans to shed jobs.
"We're determined to reverse these decisions as we head to the bargaining table with GM," he said.

Hargrove told reporters the union will try to reach a settlement with GM in the nine days before the strike deadline. But he warned it would be "very very difficult to get a settlement without a strike."

The union is considering an "escalated" strike plan if an agreement was not reached by Oct. 2, rather than striking all plants at once. This would help cushion GM Canada's 28,510 workers from the financial impact of a strike.
"We'd like to limit the exposure on our members, their families and the community, while at the same time putting maximum pressure on GM," Hargrove said.
The CAW will hold a convention on Oct. 18 to approve a special dues assessment to provide GM workers with strike pay in case of a protracted stoppage at the Oshawa, Ontario-based automaker.
Hargrove said his choice of GM as the second target in Canada will not be interfered with by the bargaining schedule of the United Auto Workers in the United States.

"We have a clear understanding between myself and Mr. (Stephen) Yokich (president) of the UAW that we will not do anything to interfere or harm one another in our efforts to put together a 1996 collective agreement," Hargrove said.
The CAW, founded in 1984 when its members broke away from the UAW, last went on strike in Canada at Ford's subsidiary for nine days in 1990. However, its longest strikes have been against GM.
